newsitem.title: UK: Britain to mount new bid to lift beef export ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain to mount new bid to lift beef export ban.

text.p: Britain is to mount a fresh attempt to end the European Union export ban on British beef within the next few days, government sources said on Monday.

They said the agriculture ministry is finalising a submission to the European Commission on a new certified herd scheme designed to ensure that exports come only from cattle which have never been in contact with mad cow disease.
An aide to Prime Minister John Major, asked when the scheme would be ready, replied: "Something within the next few days would not strike me as wholly out of court."

The new scheme would be considered by an EU veterinary committee, and then by farm ministers, who have previously been reluctant to sanction British exports in the light of evidence that mad cow disease is transmissible to humans.
If they approved it, the aide said, Britain would have cleared "the main final hurdle" in the way of a resumption of exports which have been halted since last March.
Among the first farmers to benefit from a lifting of the cull would be those in Northern Ireland where traditionally much better records of cows' histories are kept.
This would please the nine Ulster Unionist members of parliament on whom Major, stripped of his parliamentary majority by by-election losses and defections, is now dependent in some key votes.
The aide said the other obstacle to the lifting of the ban was the need for a cull of an extra 100,000 cattle seen as vulnerable to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
But in Paris, a senior British meat industry official told Reuters on Monday that this cull, which is additional to the slaughter of a million cattle last year, will begin next week.

"Everything is now in place. Several hundred herds have been inspected and the selective cull will start next week," Henry Lewis, export marketing manager for Britain's Meat and Livestock Commission, said.

The opposition Labour Party, which has made capital out of the fact that Major last year promised a partial lifing of the ban by November, warned on Monday that Britain faces a massive headache in disposing of the cattle already slaughtered.

Deputy leader John Prescott told a news conference that research by a parliamentary colleague had shown that by January less than four percent of the cattle culled last year had been disposed of by incineration.
Meanwhile, the government was using cold stores, warehouses and even the container port in his Hull constituency to store carcases and rendered-down meat and bonemeal, he said.
Prescott said Britain has just three incinerators capable of disposing of cattle carcases at sufficiently high temperatures to destroy the prion proteins associated with BSE.
Only one of these, near Southampton in southern England, has so far been given a contract to dispose of carcases, he said.
"At this rate. it will take to the year 2010 to dispose of last year's cull," Labour said in a statement.
Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg accused Prescott of scaremongering. "It is high time he stopped trying to make cheap political points out of a national crisis," he said.
